title: Infra playbook: GPU fleet & capacity, cloud accounts, networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD and runbooks
author: Alicia Moreno
content:
Overview
========

This playbook documents Redwood Inference's operational and engineering standards for running a production GPU fleet and associated infrastructure: cloud accounts and tagging, VPC and networking patterns, Terraform/IaC module usage, CI/CD and build pipelines, and runbooks for common day-2 operations and incidents. The goal is to provide a single consolidated reference for engineers and SREs to make consistent, safe changes that preserve capacity, cost controls, and reliability.

Scope and audience
------------------
- Scope: GPU fleet (hosted inference + Dedicated clusters), cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD pipelines that build and deploy infra, and runbooks for capacity operations and incident response.
- Audience: infra engineers, serving-runtime, SRE, platform, and on-call rotation members.

Owners & contacts
------------------
- Primary owner_team: engineering (Infra).
- Primary doc owner: Alicia Moreno (Infra Engineering).
- Pager escalation: infra-oncall -> infra-lead -> engops-manager.
- Slack channels: #infra-ops, #gpu-capacity, #oncall-escalations.

Key concepts and terminology
----------------------------
- GPU pool: logical group of nodes with same instance type and config (e.g., "gpu-pool-a100-40g-us-west-2").
- Reserved capacity: committed pool for Dedicated customers (no preemption).
- Preemptible/spot pool: lower-cost capacity for best-effort workloads.
- Model-serving node: VM or instance running inference containers and agent sidecars.
- Control plane vs data plane: control plane manages scheduling and config; data plane runs inference.

Capacity targets and SLOs
-------------------------
- Latency SLO (p99 generation latency): <= 350ms for 512-token typical workloads on A100 pools.
- Availability SLO: 99.95% per region for hosted API; Dedicated contracts may require 99.9%+.
- Headroom targets: maintain 20% spare capacity for bursting and failover during business hours, 40% overnight for maintenance windows.

GPU pool types and sizing guidance
----------------------------------
- Pool naming convention: <env>-<region>-<instance>-<tier> (examples: prod-usw2-a100x40g-primary).
- Recommended instance types (2026): NVIDIA A100-40GB (high-memory models), A100-80GB (large models), H100 for next-gen workloads.
- Minimum pool sizes: production pools should have >= 4 instances in a region; Dedicated pools sized to contractual throughput.
- Batching guidance: use continuous batching with max_batch_size tuned per model; default 64 for Llama-2-70B quantized variants, 16 for unquantized large models.

Cloud accounts, tagging and quotas
----------------------------------
- Account model: one infra account per region + customer-dedicated accounts for enterprise Private deployments.
- Required tags (applied at resource and instance level):
  | Key               | Example value                     | Notes |
  |-------------------|-----------------------------------|-------|
  | cost_center       | gpu-platform                      | Billing grouping |
  | env               | prod / staging / dev              | Environment scope |
  | owner_team        | eng-infra                         | Team responsible |
  | project           | inference-runtime                 | High-level project |
  | compliance_region | us-west-2 / eu-central-1         | Data residency |
- Quota checks: before any pool expansion, verify vCPUs, GPUs, ENIs, and IP addresses quotas with cloud-accounts team. Use the automated quota dashboard (link in related pages) and request increases at least 72 hours prior to scheduled expansions.

Networking and VPC design
--------------------------
- VPC topology: each region uses a hub-and-spoke model: shared-services hub (NAT, central logging), then per-pool spokes for isolation.
- Subnet layout: dedicated subnets per pool with /22 for data-plane pools to ensure IP headroom.
- Security groups: minimal surface area — allow control-plane CIDR, monitoring endpoints, and egress to model artifact storage.
- Endpoint design: use private endpoints for control-plane APIs; enable VPC endpoints for object storage and KMS.
- Egress & NAT: shared NAT instances in hub for outbound traffic, with egress rules audited quarterly.

Terraform / IaC modules and patterns
-----------------------------------
- Module registry (internal): registry.redwood/infra-modules. Primary modules used for GPU fleet:
  - redwood/gpu-pool/aws (versioned) — creates node group, autoscaling config, tagging, and IAM roles.
  - redwood/networking/vpc — hub and spoke VPC with subnet allocations.
  - redwood/cloud-accounts/account — account bootstrap config and guardrails.
  - redwood/iam/roles — service roles and least-privilege policies.
  - redwood/k8s/eks-nodegroup — EKS nodegroup wrapper used when running on Kubernetes.

- Module usage example (simplified Terraform snippet):
  ```hcl
  module "gpu_pool_primary" {
    source = "registry.redwood/infra-modules/gpu-pool/aws"
    version = "~> 2.3"

    name_prefix    = "prod-usw2-a100x40g"
    instance_type  = "nvidia_a100_40gb"
    min_size       = 4
    max_size       = 24
    spot_enabled   = true
    tags = {
      cost_center = "gpu-platform"
      env = "prod"
      owner_team = "eng-infra"
    }
  }
  ```

- Module practice rules:
  - All module versions must be pinned in env-level repo (no floating latest).
  - Changes to module public outputs must be approved via ADR and documented in CHANGELOG.
  - Use workspace-per-environment and remote state locking (S3 + DynamoDB) for AWS.

CI/CD and build pipelines
-------------------------
- Repositories:
  - infra/terraform-root (per-environment root modules and env variables)
  - infra/infra-modules (module development repository)
  - infra/pipelines (shared pipeline templates and policies)
- Pipeline engine: GitHub Actions for PR checks + Atlantis for Terraform plan/apply gating.
- Pipeline stages (typical):
  1. lint (tflint, checkov), format (terraform fmt), and unit tests (terragrunt/terratest where available).
  2. PR plan — Atlantis posts plan comment.
  3. Security scan — Checkov/opa policies enforced.
  4. Manual approval gates for changes touching prod; requires two approvers (infra-owner + security).
  5. Apply — handled by Atlantis with remote-state locking.

Build artifacts and images
- Container image builds for inference runtime are produced in infra/cicd-image-builder and pushed to internal registry (registry.redwood/inference-runtime). Images are tagged by git SHA and semantic release.

Runbooks and operational playbooks
----------------------------------
Core runbooks (links):
- GPU capacity runbook: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026
- Incident response: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process
- Upgrade and rollback: /confluence/eng-infra/upgrade-and-rollback

Common procedures (short):
1) Scale up a pool (for capacity burst)
   1. Verify quota and budget with cloud-accounts dashboard.
   2. Open a short-lived maintenance window in PagerDuty with a 30m duration label.
   3. In terraform-root repo, update min_size/max_size and run Atlantis plan.
   4. Wait for node bootstrap and run health checks: smoke tests for model-serving, p95 latency check.
   5. Monitor cost telemetry for the first 24 hours.

2) Emergency scaling (hotfix)
   1. If p99 latency spike and pool saturation detected, page infra-oncall.
   2. Oncall runs the pre-approved emergency autoscale playbook: temporarily increase max_size via remote console only if Atlantis pipeline is blocked.
   3. Reconcile Terraform as soon as possible (create PR with exact delta and run plan/apply).

3) Node image upgrade (rolling)
   1. Create a canary node group with new image in the same pool.
   2. Drain 1 instance from primary and validate model traffic on canary for 30–60 minutes.
   3. If metrics stable, roll remaining nodes in batches of 10%–25% with health checks between batches.
   4. If regressions detected, run rollback steps in section below.

Upgrade & rollback procedure (short)
------------------------------------
- Rollback steps:
  1. Revert Terraform image tag or instance template to previous known-good version in a new PR.
  2. Apply to a canary node group and validate.
  3. Scale canary and cut over routing (if applicable).
  4. If cutover successful, perform rolling update for remainder; otherwise, escalate to engops-manager and open an incident.

Monitoring, metrics and alerts
-----------------------------
- Key metrics to monitor:
  - GPU utilization (avg and p95) per pool.
  - Queue length / pending requests per node.
  - p50/p95/p99 latencies for typical prompt profiles.
  - Node bootstrap success rate and time-to-ready.
  - Cost per 1M tokens processed (derived metric).
- Example alert thresholds (initial):
  - GPU_util_p95 >= 85% for 10m -> P2 (capacity pressure).
  - Pending_requests_per_node > 100 for 5m -> P1 (immediate scale required).
  - Node_bootstrap_failure_rate > 3% in 1h -> P1 (deploy rollback/stop autoscale).

Oncall and escalation
---------------------
- Paging policy: follow the standard infra-oncall rotation. Page sequence: infra-oncall -> infra-lead -> engops-manager.
- Escalation matrix in runbook: include Slack DMs, phone numbers, and 1-hour SLA for rescue actions on P1 incidents.

Change approval checklist
-------------------------
Before merging PRs that change pools or networking ensure:
- [ ] Module version pinned and changelog updated.
- [ ] Security review (if IAM or network changes).
- [ ] Quota check and cloud-account approval.
- [ ] Load test plan for changes that affect throughput.
- [ ] Rollout plan with canaries and rollback steps.

Appendices
----------
A. Example Terraform variables table:
| variable_name       | description                              | example_value       | required |
|---------------------|------------------------------------------|---------------------|----------|
| instance_type       | Cloud instance flavor                    | nvidia_a100_40gb    | true     |
| min_size            | Minimum node count                       | 4                   | true     |
| max_size            | Maximum node count                       | 24                  | true     |
| spot_enabled        | Use spot instances for pool              | true                | false    |

B. Useful CLI snippets:
- Check node pool status (AWS example):
  aws autoscaling describe-auto-scaling-groups --query "AutoScalingGroups[?contains(Tags[?Key=='Name'].Value, 'prod-usw2-a100x40g')]"
- Drain a Kubernetes node (EKS):
  kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --timeout=5m
